title: How do half rotis add up, one after another?
description: Half rotis are collected one by one, from one half roti up to five. Each sum is written as a number of times one half. Keeko's doubt, that one half plus one half is two fourths, is broken.
teaching_notes: One idea: collecting the same fractional unit again and again is counting that unit, so the unit stays the same and only the count grows. Watch for students who add the bottom numbers as well.

source: Using half rotis, write 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 halves as addition statements.
video_script.why: The child collects half rotis one at a time, writes each collection as an addition, and sees that adding the same unit counts the units.
video_script.substitution: Add one more half roti each time and write the sum as the number of halves, times one half.
video_script.anchor: A row of five half rotis next to one full roti, collected one at a time
video_script.wrong_answer: one half plus one half is two fourths
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko adds the bottom numbers as well and says one half plus one half is two fourths. Two halves fill one full roti, and two fourths is not a full roti, so the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: Adding halves counts how many halves we have

final_answer.spoken: one half is one times half, and two, three, four and five halves added are two, three, four and five times half

video_script.fraction_reading: one half, two halves, three halves, four halves, five halves, two fourths
never_show: 2/4 as the sum of two halves
maths_rules: a full roti is the whole; a half roti is the fractional unit 1/2
check: 2 halves make 1 full roti and 4 halves make 2 full rotis
slip: adding the bottom numbers gives 2/4, which is half a roti, not the full roti that two halves make
video_script.design: One idea: adding the same unit again and again counts the unit. Assumes one half and one fourth from the strip videos. Wrong idea: adding the bottom numbers too. The row of half rotis stays on the board to the end.
